terms.sub: Classification and Properties of Sensory Receptors
terms.term: Muller's law of specific nerve energies
clues: Also known as the labeled-line principle, it explains why pressing on a closed eye evokes flashes of light
Because action potentials are identical across neurons, modality depends on central pathway termination
It states that stimulating a sensory pathway always produces its characteristic sensation regardless of stimulus type

terms.sub: Sensory Transduction, Receptor Potential, and Adaptation
clues: Also called a generator potential, it is graded in amplitude and decays electrotonically
Unlike an action potential, it lacks a refractory period and can summate temporally or spatially
When it depolarizes the first node of Ranvier to threshold, it triggers propagated action potentials

terms.sub: Sensory Transduction, Receptor Potential, and Adaptation
clues: It compresses a vast range of stimulus strengths so receptors stay sensitive without saturating
It explains why adding one candle in a dark room is obvious while adding one in sunlight goes unnoticed
It states that perceived sensation intensity is proportional to the logarithm of physical stimulus intensity
It operates in dorsal column nuclei, thalamus, cortex, retina, and auditory pathways
Strongly excited central neurons activate inhibitory interneurons to suppress adjacent neighbors
It sharpens center-surround spatial contrast and improves two-point tactile discrimination
Proposed by Melzack and Wall, it explains why rubbing an injured shin or using TENS relieves pain
Large myelinated A-beta mechanoreceptors excite inhibitory interneurons in lamina II (substantia gelatinosa)
This dorsal horn circuit suppresses nociceptive transmission from A-delta and C pain fibers
Myocardial ischemia felt in the medial left arm and diaphragmatic irritation felt at the shoulder tip are classic examples
It occurs because visceral and somatic nociceptors converge onto shared dorsal horn spinothalamic neurons
The somatosensory cortex mislocalizes deep organ pain to the corresponding embryonic skin dermatome

terms.sub: Muscle Spindles and the Stretch (Myotatic) Reflex
clues: Upper motor neurons simultaneously excite both extrafusal and intrafusal motor neurons during movement
It keeps the central equatorial region of the muscle spindle taut as the whole muscle shortens
Without it, voluntary muscle contraction would unload the spindle and silence Type Ia sensory feedback

terms.sub: Muscle Spindles and the Stretch (Myotatic) Reflex
clues: In the patellar reflex, quadriceps Type Ia afferents excite glycinergic interneurons to relax the hamstrings
It prevents antagonist muscles from opposing agonist contraction during a stretch reflex or movement
It relies on spinal Ia inhibitory interneurons

terms.sub: Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron Lesions and Spinal Shock
clues: It occurs immediately after an acute complete spinal cord transection due to loss of descending tonic facilitation
During this phase, all somatic and autonomic reflexes below the lesion are absent with flaccid paralysis
Weeks later it resolves into spasticity, hyperreflexia, and return of the bulbocavernosus reflex
